teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Latin can put **cum** in front of a verb in the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do), and the clause then gives the *reason* for the rest of the sentence. That is **cum + subjunctive meaning 'since' (or, with tamen, 'although')**. In *Cum aeger sim, in cubiculō maneō* the cum clause says why I stay in the bedroom: because I am ill. Read 'since' for cum and see whether the sentence makes sense.

check.ask: Does this cum clause tell you when the boys keep quiet, or why?

teach.title: The mood is the tell-tale
teach.say: Plain *cum* with an indicative verb (the everyday statement form) means 'when' or 'whenever'. Put that verb into the subjunctive and *cum* can give the reason instead. Look at the one verb inside the clause: *verberat* is indicative, 'he is beating'; *verberet* is subjunctive, and the clause becomes 'since he is beating'. In a story about the past the same subjunctive *cum* is the 'when' of chapter 28; with a present main verb, as here, it is the reason.

check.ask: fugiat is subjunctive, not fugit. What does that make the cum clause?

teach.title: Not the preposition cum
teach.say: The other *cum* is a preposition and means 'with'. Telling them apart needs no grammar: the preposition is followed by a noun in the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) and owns no verb — *cum Aemiliā*, *cum Dāvō*. The causal *cum* owns a verb, and that verb is subjunctive. Both can stand in the same sentence.

check.ask: Is this cum the preposition 'with', or the one that means 'since'?

teach.title: With tamen it means 'although'
teach.say: If *tamen* ('nevertheless') stands in the other clause, the same *cum* clause stops being a reason and becomes a concession: you grant something and then go against it. *Cum Iūlia parva sit, tamen fortis est* — although Julia is small, she is nevertheless brave. The cum clause itself is built exactly as before; *tamen* does the work.

check.ask: tamen stands in the main clause: does cum mean 'since' here, or 'although'?

teach.title: Present now, imperfect for the past
teach.say: The tense inside the cum clause follows the main verb. A present main verb takes the present subjunctive: *plōrat, cum pater absit*. A past main verb takes the imperfect subjunctive (the '-rem, -ret' subjunctive, built on the infinitive): *plōrābat, cum pater abesset*. In past time this is also the shape of the story *cum* of chapter 28, so ask what the clause is doing: if it answers *why*, read 'since'; if it only says *when*, read 'while'.

check.ask: The main verb tacēbant is past. Put timeō into the tense the cum clause needs.

teach.title: Say one yourself
teach.say: Now add a reason to a statement. Keep the main clause as it is, write *cum*, then the subject, then its verb in the subjunctive — present if the main verb is present. *Syra Iūliam amat* plus a reason gives *Syra Iūliam amat, cum bona puella sit*.

check.ask: Complete the reason: put aegrōtō into the present subjunctive.

core.text: A reason for the main clause can be given by **cum + subjunctive meaning 'since' (or, with tamen, 'although')**: *plōrō, cum mortua sit* — I weep, since she is dead. Unlike the story-telling *cum*, it works in any tense: the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come) after a present main verb, the imperfect after a past one. With *tamen* (nevertheless) in the main clause it is a concession: *cum dīves sit, tamen miser est* — although he is rich, he is unhappy. Latin name: *cum causāle et concessīvum*.
*Since* and *because* give a reason; *although* admits something and then goes against it. One Latin word does both jobs; the subjunctive marks it.
cum + subjunctive = since / because; cum … tamen = although; quippe quī + subjunctive = 'as one who', another way of giving a reason.

invented.la: Cum pecūniam nōn habeam, pānem emere nōn possum.
invented.en: Since I have no money, I cannot buy bread.

invented.la: Cum servus sit, tamen līber esse vidētur.
invented.en: Although he is a slave, he nevertheless seems free.

core.text: Story *cum* appears only with the imperfect or pluperfect in a past narrative and tells you *when*. If the cum verb is present or perfect subjunctive, or the clause answers *why*, it is causal. Test by translating 'since': if it fits, causal.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: *cum* followed by a noun in the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form) is just 'with' — *cum Dāvō ambulat*. A causal *cum* has its own verb in the subjunctive.

The learner's notes: the causal subjunctive is usually introduced by *cum*, 'effectively making it mean since or because' — *audīmus, cum ipse loquāris* (we listen, because you yourself are speaking), *ambulāmus, cum nōn sit nōbīs equus*. A relative clause can do it too, often with *quippe* to make it clear: *sitiō quippe quī nūllam aquam habeam* — I am thirsty, as one who has no water.

For a finished reason after a present verb the perfect subjunctive is used (Week 10): *nōn possum exīre cum aliquis portam clauserit* — I cannot go out since someone has shut the gate; after a past verb the pluperfect: *nōn poteram exīre cum … clausisset*. *cum* + indicative still means plain 'when(ever)': *gaudeō cum dē līberīs cōgitō*. Ørberg writes 'although' with *quamquam* + indicative (*quamquam valdē dolēbat, tamen …*); *cum … tamen* is the subjunctive version of the same idea.
